Hydrodynamic regulation drives azo dye transformation and hydrolysis 
acidification by reshaping microbial metabolism in the micro-aerobic 
hydrolysis acidification reactor

Keywords:

Metabolic mechanism
A B S T R A C T
Acid Red GR is a representative sulfonated azo dye frequently detected in dyeing wastewater, yet the role of 
hydrodynamic conditions in regulating its biodegradation in micro-aerobic hydrolysis acidification (MAHA) 
systems remains unclear. This study investigated how hydrodynamic conditions drive Acid Red GR trans­
formation, hydrolysis acidification, and microbial metabolic responses in the MAHA reactor. The results showed 
that a moderate stirring speed of 120 rad/min (R2) balanced turbulence intensity and flow uniformity, with 
relatively high oxygen transfer, a favorable micro-aerobic niche, and the highest biodegradability (0.50) and 
volatile fatty acid (VFA) production (140.38 mg/L). This hydrodynamic condition enriched hydrolytic, facul­
tative, and fermentative genera, including Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Bacteroides, Propionivibrio, and Bacillus, and 
was associated with higher abundances of genes encoding enzymes involved in azo reduction, aromatic inter­
mediate transformation, pyruvate generation, and acidogenic metabolism. Integrated metagenomic, metab­
olomic, and functional group evidence further indicated that Acid Red GR degradation proceeded through azo 
reduction, deamination, desulfonation, aromatic ring cleavage, and subsequent acidogenesis. These findings

demonstrate that hydrodynamic optimization regulates MAHA performance by coordinating oxygen transfer, 
microbial niche formation, and metabolic functional potential, providing a mechanistic basis for enhancing the 
biodegradability and treatment efficiency of dyeing wastewater.
1. Introduction
Acid Red GR is a representative sulfonated azo dye contaminant 
frequently detected in dyeing wastewater [1]. Its highly conjugated azo 
structure and sulfonated aromatic framework contribute to persistent 
coloration, limited biodegradability, and resistance to conventional 
biological treatment [2]. Moreover, incomplete transformation of azo 
dyes may lead to the accumulation of aromatic amines and other in­
termediates with potential ecological risks [3]. Therefore, developing 
effective strategies that not only remove dye color but also promote 
complete molecular transformation and detoxification of azo dye con­
taminants remains an important challenge in wastewater treatment.
Micro-aerobic hydrolysis acidification (MAHA) has recently emerged 
as a promising biological approach for enhancing azo dye trans­
formation and improving wastewater biodegradability [1,4]. Unlike 
conventional anaerobic hydrolysis acidification, MAHA introduces trace 
oxygen to maintain a dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration of 
0.1–1.0 mg/L, creating a micro-aerobic environment that may simulta­
neously facilitate anaerobic azo-bond reduction, aerobic oxidation of 
aromatic intermediates, and microbial carbon metabolism [5,6]. Previ­
ous studies have shown that MAHA can achieve over 80% azo dye 
decolorization, substantial organic matter removal (30–55%), and 
enhanced biodegradability (BOD5/COD = 0.36–0.50), while promoting 
volatile fatty acid (VFA) production and the further transformation of 
refractory 
aromatic 
intermediates 
through 
processes 
such 
as 
aromatic-ring cleavage [1,7,8]. However, within this narrow oxygen 
range, even subtle variations in the local micro-aerobic environment 
may substantially affect redox conditions and biological responses [9]. 
Thus, understanding microenvironmental regulation is critical for 
optimizing MAHA performance.
Hydrodynamic conditions play a critical role in shaping the micro- 
aerobic environments characteristic of MAHA systems [10,11]. By 
regulating gas-liquid mass transfer, bubble dispersion, and oxygen 
transport, hydrodynamics can reshape the local microenvironments 
experienced by functional microorganisms and consequently affect their 
metabolic activity and pollutant transformation [12–14]. Existing 
studies on hydrolysis acidification reactors have shown that hydrody­
namic optimization can improve mixing, mitigate dead zones and 
short-circuiting, and enhance treatment performance [15,16]. However, 
the specific role of hydrodynamics in regulating micro-aerobic envi­
ronments in MAHA systems remains insufficiently resolved, and hy­
drodynamic investigation has therefore been proposed as an important 
direction for future research [17]. This issue is particularly important 
because recent MAHA studies have demonstrated that changes in 
micro-aerobic conditions can substantially alter microbial communities, 
functional genes, metabolic pathways, and the transformation of re­
fractory organic matter [1,4]. For azo dyes, Acid Red GR has been 
proposed to undergo azo-bond reduction, desulfonation, hydrolytic 
deamination, aromatic-ring cleavage, and subsequent conversion 
through 
central 
carbon 
metabolism 
[1]. 
However, 
different 
micro-aerobic conditions have been reported to result in two distinct 
pollutant transformation pathways, dominated by hydroxylation and 
deamination, respectively [9]. Corresponding changes were also 
observed in microbial functions, including genes and enzymes involved 
in phenolic oxidation and aromatic-ring cleavage. Therefore, eluci­
dating microbial metabolism and azo dye degradation mechanisms in 
MAHA systems remains a important issue that requires further 
investigation.
Resolving these mechanisms requires an integrated approach that 
links hydrodynamic regulation with microbial metabolic responses and 
molecular transformation of azo dyes. Metagenomic analysis can char­
acterize microbial functional potential, whereas liquid chromatography- 
mass spectrometry (LC-MS)-based metabolite identification can reveal 
transformation intermediates [18,19]. However, these approaches do 
not directly resolve the relative sequence in which functional groups 
respond to hydrodynamic perturbation. Two-dimensional correlation 
spectroscopy (2D-COS), with turbulence intensity used as a continuous 
external perturbation, can complement these analyses by enhancing the 
resolution of overlapping Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy 
(FTIR) bands and determining the relative response sequence of func­
tional groups [4,20]. Although hydrodynamic analysis, metagenomic 
analysis, LC-MS-based metabolite identification, and 2D-COS have each 
been applied in related environmental and bioprocess studies [18,21], 
their integration for resolving hydrodynamic-microbial-molecular in­
teractions in MAHA systems remains limited. Such integration is needed 
to connect reactor-scale flow characteristics and oxygen transfer with 
microbial functional responses, metabolite profiles, and the structural 
transformation of dye-derived organics.
This study examined how hydrodynamic conditions regulate the 
biodegradation pathway and metabolic transformation of Acid Red GR 
in the MAHA reactor treating dyeing wastewater. Reactor-scale flow 
characteristics were resolved using the Euler-Euler two-fluid model, 
while the corresponding oxygen transfer responses were quantified 
experimentally. Process performance and EPS characteristics were 
further evaluated to characterize dye transformation, biodegradability 
improvement, and acidogenic behavior under different hydrodynamic 
conditions. Metagenomic analysis and LC-MS-based metabolite identi­
fication were integrated with 2D-COS to relate microbial functional 
potential and transformation intermediates to the response sequence of 
functional groups. These complementary datasets were further used to 
elucidate Acid Red GR degradation and acidogenic pathways and to 
clarify the links among flow regulation, oxygen transfer, microbial 
metabolism, and dye-derived organic matter transformation in the 
MAHA system. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for hydro­
dynamic regulation of MAHA pretreatment by linking flow and oxygen 
transfer with microbial metabolism and dye-derived molecular 
transformation.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Setup and operation of the MAHA reactor
Four identical plexiglass MAHA reactors were operated in parallel at 
ambient laboratory temperature. Each reactor had an internal diameter 
of 23.4 cm, a height of 70.0 cm and an effective volume of 25 L (Fig. S1). 
The reactors were equipped with stirring, aeration, influent and effluent 
systems, and an online DO monitoring system. Air was delivered to each 
reactor via an aeration disc after passing through a flowmeter and gas 
chamber. The aeration holes had a diameter of 0.16 mm and were 
spaced 10 mm apart. Polyurethane carriers (1 × 1 × 1 cm) were used as 
biofilm supports, with a filling ratio of 30% based on the effective 
reactor volume.
Seed sludge was collected from the secondary clarifier of the Xi’an 
Fifth Wastewater Treatment Plant. Before inoculation, the sludge was 
acclimated for 3–5 d with synthetic domestic wastewater at a C:N:P ratio 
of 100:5:1, and the sludge concentration was adjusted to 
3000–4000 mg/L before introduction into the four reactors. During 
start-up, DO was controlled at 0.1–0.3 mg/L until treatment perfor­
mance stabilized and biofilms were established.
The synthetic dyeing wastewater was prepared based on a survey of

water quality at a dyeing wastewater treatment plant in Zhejiang 
Province, China. Acid Red GR and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) were added 
at 30 and 300 mg/L, respectively, while polyethylene glycol 4000, so­
dium dodecyl sulfate, sodium dodecyl sulfonate, and glucose were each 
added at 100 mg/L. Nitrogen, phosphorus, trace elements, and other 
nutrients were dosed according to a previously reported method [1]. To 
establish different hydrodynamic conditions, stirring speeds were set at 
100, 120, 140, and 160 rad/min for R1, R2, R3, and R4, respectively, 
with 100 rad/min identified experimentally as the critical stirring speed 
for carrier fluidization. During operation, the hydraulic retention time 
(HRT) was 8 h, with an aeration rate of 0.6 m3/(h⋅m3). The DO, 
oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), and pH were monitored, while 
influent and effluent chemical oxygen demand (COD), volatile fatty 
acids (VFAs), PVA, color, and five-day biochemical oxygen demand 
(BOD5) were measured.
2.2. Flow characteristic simulation methods
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were performed in 
ANSYS Fluent software to resolve the hydrodynamic characteristics of 
the MAHA reactor. A 1:1 three-dimensional model (Fig. S2a) was con­
structed based on the experimental MAHA reactor and simplified for 
numerical simulation. The geometry was meshed in ICEM software 
using unstructured grids, and grid independence analysis showed that 
221,318 cells were sufficient for reliable simulation (Fig. S2b).
The reactor contained gas, liquid, and suspended biofilm carriers. To 
reduce model complexity, the dyeing wastewater and biofilm carriers 
were treated as an equivalent continuous phase, because the carriers 
were mainly transported with the bulk liquid flow and the present work 
focused on gas dispersion, liquid mixing, and oxygen transfer rather 
than carrier-scale collision or trajectory dynamics. Therefore, the 
simulated system was simplified as a gas-liquid two-phase flow. The 
Euler-Euler two-fluid model was used to describe the gas and equivalent 
liquid phases, and the mass and momentum conservation equations 
were solved for each phase to characterize phase distribution, flow 
transport, and interphase momentum exchange (Table S1). The realiz­
able k-ε turbulence model was applied to resolve turbulent flow char­
acteristics. A population balance model (PBM) was further coupled with 
the CFD framework to account for bubble coalescence and breakup, 
which determine bubble size distribution and gas-liquid interfacial area 
(Table S1). The CFD-PBM coupled model was benchmarked against 
experimental hydrodynamic data from a similar reactor [22], and the 
model predictions showed reasonable agreement with the reported 
measurements (Fig. S2c). Because the experimental data were obtained 
from a similar rather than the present reactor, this comparison should be 
regarded as indirect rather than reactor-specific validation.
2.3. Oxygen mass transfer measurement
DO in the reactor was continuously monitored at 1 -min intervals 
using a four-channel optical fiber measuring instrument (OXY-4 SMA 
trace, PreSens GmbH, Regensburg, Germany). Anhydrous sodium sulfite 
was first added to deplete DO, after which aeration was initiated and the 
DO recovery to saturation was recorded. The volumetric oxygen mass 
transfer coefficient (kLa) was calculated from the DO recovery curve 
according to Liu et al. (2026) [23]. The standard oxygen mass transfer 
rate (SOTR) and standard oxygen mass transfer efficiency (SOTE) were 
further calculated using the saturated DO concentration under standard 
conditions and the aeration rate [24]. Under stable operation, the oxy­
gen mass transfer rate (OTR) was assumed to be equal to the microbial 
oxygen uptake rate (OUR) [25]. After aeration was stopped, the decline 
in DO was mainly attributed to microbial oxygen consumption. There­
fore, OUR was calculated from the slope of the DO-time curve during the 
non-aeration phase and was used as the steady-state OTR.
2.4. Water quality analysis
ORP and pH were measured using a portable Hach meter (Hach, 
USA). COD and BOD5 were determined using the potassium dichromate 
method and the five-day incubation method, respectively, as previously 
reported [4]. Dye concentration and color variation were characterized 
by measuring absorbance at 509 nm using a UV–visible spectropho­
tometer. PVA concentration was determined by UV spectrophotometry 
at 680 nm and calculated from a standard curve [1]. VFAs were analyzed 
using a PerkinElmer Altus high-performance liquid chromatography 
(HPLC) system equipped with an Aminex HPX-87H column (300 ×
7.8 mm; Bio-Rad, USA). Before injection, samples were filtered through 
a 0.22 μm membrane and degassed for 15 min. A 0.005 mol/L H₂SO₄ 
solution was used as the mobile phase at a flow rate of 0.6 mL/min. 
Individual VFA species were identified based on their retention times 
and quantified according to the corresponding peak areas using external 
calibration curves.
The fluorescence characteristics of influent and effluent dissolved 
organic matter (DOM) were measured using a high-sensitivity integrated 
fluorescence spectrometer (FluoroMax-4, HORIBA Scientific, USA). The 
excitation and emission wavelength ranges were 240–550 nm and 
290–600 nm, respectively, with a step size of 5 nm and a slit width of 
3 nm. Based on excitation-emission matrix (EEM) data, fluorescence 
regional integration was used to quantitatively analyze different fluo­
rescent DOM components, according to previous research [26].
2.5. EPS extraction and characterization
Biofilm was collected from the carriers by manual squeezing. EPS 
fractions, including soluble EPS (SL-EPS), loosely bound EPS (LB-EPS) 
and tightly bound EPS (TB-EPS), were extracted from the biofilm using a 
thermal extraction method [27]. Proteins (PN) and polysaccharides (PS) 
in EPS were determined using the modified Folin-Lowry method and the 
anthrone method, respectively [28].
2.6. Functional group characterization
EPS samples from different layers were scanned using a Fourier 
transform infrared spectrometer (VERTEX 70, Bruker, Germany) over 
the range of 4000–400 cm−1. Functional groups were qualitatively 
identified according to peak positions. 2D-COS was then used to analyze 
the response characteristics of these functional groups under flow 
perturbation. The raw spectra were processed by baseline correction, 
smoothing and normalization. Turbulence intensity was used as the 
external continuous perturbation variable to construct synchronous and 
asynchronous two-dimensional correlation spectra. The response 
sequence of characteristic functional groups was determined from the 
sign relationship between synchronous and asynchronous peaks ac­
cording to Noda’s rules [29].
2.7. Metagenomic analysis
At the end of each operating condition, carriers were collected from 
several positions within the reactor. Biofilms detached from these car­
riers were combined and thoroughly homogenized to obtain one com­
posite sample for each condition. Accordingly, four composite biofilm 
samples corresponding to R1-R4 were subjected to metagenomic anal­
ysis. The samples were stored at −80 ◦C before DNA extraction. Total 
genomic DNA was extracted using a commercial biofilm DNA extraction 
kit, and DNA concentration, purity, and integrity were evaluated prior to 
library preparation. Qualified DNA was fragmented for paired-end li­
brary construction and subsequently subjected to high-throughput 
sequencing on an Illumina platform (Personalbio, Shanghai, China). 
Raw sequencing reads were filtered to remove adapter sequences, low- 
quality reads, and short sequences, followed by de novo assembly 
using MEGAHIT. Coding sequences were predicted using Prodigal, and

the predicted genes were clustered to generate a nonredundant gene 
catalog. Gene abundances were estimated by mapping the quality- 
filtered reads to the gene catalog. Functional annotation was per­
formed against the KEGG database to obtain KEGG Orthology (KO) and 
pathway information. Genes annotated as encoding enzymes potentially 
involved in Acid Red GR transformation and acidogenesis were subse­
quently screened, and their relative abundances and taxonomic affilia­
tions were used to evaluate the functional potential of different 
microbial taxa.
2.8. Metabolite detection and identification
Samples for metabolite analysis were collected from each reactor 
(R1-R4) at the end of operation and analyzed by LC-MS. After thawing at 
4 ◦C, samples were extracted with methanol and centrifuged at 
12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 ◦C. The supernatants were dried, recon­
stituted in 150 μL of 2-chloro-L-phenylalanine solution (4 ppm in 80% 
methanol–water), and filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane.
Metabolites were analyzed using an Agilent 1290 Infinity LC system 
coupled with an AB SCIEX TripleTOF 6600 mass spectrometer.

Separation was performed on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH Amide column 
(1.7 μm, 2.1 × 100 mm) at 25 ◦C using 25 mM ammonium acetate and 
25 mM ammonium hydroxide in water (A) and acetonitrile (B) at 
0.5 mL/min. A 12-min gradient from 95% to 40% B was applied, fol­
lowed by re-equilibration. Mass spectra were acquired in positive and 
negative electrospray ionization modes, with TOF-MS and MS/MS scan 
ranges of m/z 60–1000 and 25–1000, respectively. Raw data were 
converted using ProteoWizard and processed with XCMS. Metabolites 
were identified based on accurate mass (error < 25 ppm), retention 
time, MS/MS fragmentation, and collision-energy information against 
an in-house database, followed by manual verification.
2.9. Statistical Analysis
Correlation networks among functional bacteria, key enzymes, and 
metabolites were constructed in Python using pandas, scipy.stats, net­
workx, and matplotlib. Mantel tests were performed in R to assess re­
lationships among environmental factors, microbial communities, 
enzymes, and metabolites. Pearson correlations with |r| > 0.5 were 
considered strong. Group differences were evaluated using one-way 
ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD test or the Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn- 
Holm correction, as appropriate. Statistical significance was set at 
p < 0.05, and different lowercase letters indicated significant differences 
among groups.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Hydrodynamic characteristics under different stirring conditions
Increasing stirring speed progressively altered the gas-phase flow 
field, as reflected by increases in gas-phase velocity, turbulent kinetic 
energy, and turbulent viscosity (Fig. 1). These changes indicated 
enhanced gas-liquid mixing and momentum exchange under stronger 
stirring. However, the higher stirring conditions (R3 and R4) generated 
more pronounced local peaks in velocity and turbulence-related pa­
rameters, suggesting increased spatial heterogeneity of the flow field. 
Such localized high-velocity and high-turbulence regions may promote 
rapid bubble transport and increase local shear, potentially altering the 
spatial persistence and distribution of oxygen within the reactor. In 
contrast, R2 maintained sufficient flow intensity while exhibiting a more 
continuous distribution of turbulent viscosity, indicating a more 
spatially uniform hydrodynamic field. Compared with the higher stir­
ring conditions, R2 therefore provided a relatively favorable combina­
tion of flow intensity and spatial uniformity. Because direct 
hydrodynamic measurements were not available for validation in the 
present reactor, the CFD results were interpreted primarily in terms of 
relative differences among R1-R4 rather than as exact predictions of 
local hydrodynamic quantities. The experimentally determined oxygen- 
transfer responses were subsequently used as independent evidence to 
evaluate whether the hydrodynamic differences predicted by CFD were 
associated with changes in gas-liquid oxygen transfer.

3.2. Oxygen mass transfer characteristics
Oxygen mass transfer showed a nonlinear response to increasing 
turbulence intensity (Figs. 2a-2c). The kLa, SOTR, and SOTE increased 
from 0.21 h−1, 0.38 g/h, and 0.84% in R1 to 0.24 h−1, 0.42 g/h, and 
0.95% in R2, respectively. These parameters changed only slightly from 
R2 to R3 and subsequently decreased to 0.23 h−1, 0.40 g/h and 0.91% in 
R4. OTR showed a similar trend, increasing from 1.21 mg/(L⋅h) in R1 to 
1.37 and 1.39 mg/(L⋅h) in R2 and R3, respectively, before decreasing to 
1.29 mg/(L⋅h) in R4. This trend was consistent with previous research, 
in which oxygen transfer performance was significantly affected by 
turbulence intensity and an effective stirring speed range was observed 
[30]. In the present system, oxygen transfer was enhanced from R1 to 
R2, whereas further increases in stirring intensity produced little addi­
tional improvement in R3. The decline observed in R4 may be associated 
with the stronger and more heterogeneous flow field identified in 
Section 3.1, which could accelerate bubble transport and gas escape and 
shorten effective gas-liquid contact time [31].
The DO concentration increased progressively across R1-R4 
(Fig. S3), reaching 0.11 ± 0.01, 0.14 ± 0.02, 0.18 ± 0.02, and 0.24 
± 0.04 mg/L, respectively. This was close to the 0.18 ± 0.05 mg/L re­
ported for a micro-aerated upflow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) 
reactor treating synthetic textile wastewater [32], indicating that the 
present system operated within a comparable low-DO micro-aerobic 
regime. Despite the progressive increase in bulk DO from R2 to R4, 
oxygen transfer showed only limited further improvement, indicating 
that bulk DO alone did not determine oxygen transfer performance. R2 
achieved oxygen transfer comparable to R3 at a lower DO level while 
maintaining a more uniform flow field, suggesting that moderate stirring 
provided a favorable balance between oxygen delivery and flow 
uniformity.
3.3. Pollutant transformation and acidogenesis
The pollutant transformation characteristics under different stirring 
conditions are shown in Fig. 3. Decolorization efficiencies remained 
consistently high across R1-R4, ranging from 87.13% to 89.38%, with 
no significant differences among the reactors (p = 0.122; Fig. 3a). The 
consistently high decolorization across R1-R4 suggested that the low- 
oxygen conditions were sufficient to sustain effective azo-dye trans­
formation, which was further supported by the azo reduction-related 
functional potential identified in Section 3.8. In parallel, 3D-EEM fluo­
rescence spectroscopy revealed substantial transformation of DOM 
during MAHA treatment (Fig. S4). The influent exhibited distinct fluo­
rescence signals in regions II, III, IV, and V, corresponding to aromatic 
protein-like, fulvic acid-like, soluble microbial byproduct-like, and 
humic acid-like substances, respectively. These fluorescence signals 
were markedly attenuated after treatment, indicating substantial 
transformation of fluorescent organic constituents. In contrast to the 
high and relatively stable decolorization, COD and PVA removal effi­
ciencies remained comparatively low across all reactors, ranging from 
18.86% to 22.19% and 16.68–18.61%, respectively (Fig. 3b-c), consis­
tent with values reported for other MAHA systems [1]. This apparent 
discrepancy between efficient decolorization and limited COD removal 
suggests that MAHA primarily promoted structural transformation and 
partial conversion of refractory organics rather than complete miner­
alization. In particular, azo-dye cleavage and subsequent hydro­
lysis/acidification can convert complex organic structures into smaller 
and more biodegradable intermediates [7]. Accordingly, wastewater 
biodegradability increased markedly after MAHA treatment (Fig. 3d). 
Notably, the BOD5/COD ratio in R2 reached 0.50, exceeding the value 
reported in a previous MAHA study [4], where BOD5/COD increased 
from 0.32 to 0.36. Collectively, these results indicate that the MAHA 
process effectively transformed refractory organic constituents into

more biodegradable forms while maintaining high decolorization effi­
ciency, with R2 showing a particularly favorable overall transformation 
pattern.
VFA production further supported the observed improvement in 
wastewater biodegradability (Fig. 3e). Acetate was the dominant VFA, 
accounting for 79.4%-88.1% of total VFAs, followed by propionate at 
11.8%-20.6%. Total VFA production differed significantly among the 
four operating conditions, with R2 showing the highest average con­
centration of 140.38 mg/L and significantly higher VFA production than 
R1, R3, and R4 (p < 0.05). Meanwhile, propionate concentration also 
varied significantly among the operating conditions (Fig. 3f), with the 
highest mean value of 28.88 mg/L observed in R2. VFAs are key in­
termediates generated during the hydrolysis and acidification of com­
plex organic substrates and can therefore serve as indicators of 
acidogenic conversion [33]. The enhanced VFA accumulation in R2, 
together with its higher BOD5/COD ratio, suggested that the hydrody­
namic conditions under R2 were associated with more effective con­
version of complex organic matter into soluble, biodegradable 
acidogenic products. Notably, the highest VFA production did not 
coincide with the highest bulk DO or the strongest stirring condition, but 
occurred under the moderate stirring condition of R2. This observation 
further suggested that excessive stirring and bulk DO did not necessarily 
enhance acidogenic conversion, highlighting the importance of main­
taining an appropriate balance between oxygen availability and 
hydrodynamic conditions during MAHA.
3.4. EPS content and composition
EPS are not only microbial metabolic products but also key matrices 
for cell adhesion, biofilm growth and extracellular reactions [34]. In 
MAHA systems, EPS can adsorb dye-derived organic matter and provide 
microenvironments for extracellular enzymatic transformation, thereby 
facilitating the release of smaller soluble products into the supernatant 
[35]. As shown in Fig. 4a, R2 had the lowest SL-EPS proportion (48%) 
and the highest TB-EPS proportion (34%) among the reactors, indicating 
a shift from loosely bound EPS toward a more compact EPS structure. 
This restructuring may have improved biofilm stability and extracellular 
enzyme retention [36]. In addition, PN was the dominant component in 
all EPS layers, accounting for more than 75.8% (Fig. 4b). The PN/PS 
ratio, which reflected surface hydrophobicity and aggregation stability 
of sludge flocs or biofilms [37], remained around 3.4 in R1-R3 but 
decreased slightly in R4. This was likely caused by excessive shear, 
which mildly disrupted EPS structure and reduced floc stability [38]. 
These results indicated that R2 developed a more compact and stable 
EPS matrix, which may have improved extracellular enzyme retention 
and supported organic matter transformation and acidogenesis.

3.5. Hydrodynamic regulation of functional group responses
The FTIR spectra of EPS showed similar characteristic peaks within 
4000–400 cm⁻¹ (Fig. S5), mainly involving O–H, N–H, C–O–C, –N = N–, 
S––O, benzene ring and substituted benzene structures. The band at 
3200–3600 cm⁻¹ was assigned to O–H and N–H stretching vibrations 
[39]. The peaks at 2850–2950 cm⁻¹ corresponded to –CH₃ and –CH₂– 
stretching vibrations [40], reflecting aliphatic organic components and 
protein side chains. The region at 1600–1650 cm⁻¹ was associated with 
aromatic C––C, amide C––O and azo bond (–N = N–) vibrations [40]. 
The bands at 1400–1550 cm⁻¹ were attributed to –CH₃ and –CH₂– 
bending vibrations and aromatic skeleton vibrations. The absorption 
band near 1360 cm⁻¹ was related to O–H bending vibrations in phenolic 
or alcoholic groups [41]. The 1000–1250 cm⁻¹ region represented C–O, 
C–O–C and S––O stretching vibrations, mainly reflecting EPS poly­
saccharides and sulfonic groups in dye molecules [42]. The 
700–800 cm⁻¹ region was assigned to out of plane bending vibrations of 
benzene rings and substituted benzene structures [43]. The increased 
intensity of the 700–800 cm⁻¹ bands in R2-R4 suggested greater expo­
sure or accumulation of benzene ring and substituted benzene structures 
during dye degradation.
To further examine the response sequence of functional groups to 
flow structure in MAHA systems, synchronous (Fig. 4c) and asynchro­
nous (Fig. 4d) 2D-COS spectra were obtained over the range of 
4000–400 cm-1. In the synchronous spectrum, autocorrelation was 
observed for almost all major peaks, with the strongest peaks at 1023, 
1624 and 3414 cm⁻¹ . The results showed that C–O/C–O–C, –N = N– and 
O–H/N–H were highly responsive to flow field variations. Cross peaks 
among the main functional groups were observed in the asynchronous 
spectrum, indicating that the transformation of these groups in dyeing 
wastewater did not occur simultaneously. According to Noda’s rules 
[29], the signs of synchronous and asynchronous cross peaks were used 
to determine the response sequence of the main functional groups 
(Table 
S2), 
which 
followed 
the 
order 
of 
1624 > 1456 > 1360 > 670 = 772 ≈1186 cm⁻¹ . The first response at 
1624 cm⁻¹ indicated that azo bond related conjugated structures were 
preferentially affected under different turbulence intensities. This was 
followed by the rearrangement of aliphatic side chains (1456 cm⁻¹) and 
the bending of phenolic or alcoholic O–H (1360 cm⁻¹). In contrast, the 
later responses of the bands at 670 and 772 cm⁻¹ , together with the 
1186 cm⁻¹ band, suggested that substituted aromatic structures and 
S––O containing functional environments were relatively less sensitive 
to changes in stirring conditions. These observations are consistent with 
a transformation sequence in which chromophore-associated and con­
jugated structures respond earlier, whereas changes involving aromatic 
substituents and sulfur-containing groups occur at later stages. Never­
theless, the 2D-COS results primarily describe the relative spectral 
response sequence and should not be interpreted as direct evidence for 
the exact order of individual chemical-bond cleavage or desulfonation 
reactions.

3.6. Microbial community composition
Microbial community composition was analyzed at both phylum and 
genus levels. Proteobacteria was the dominant phylum in all reactors, 
accounting for 72.91%-87.66% (Fig. 5a). Notably, its relative abun­
dance was the lowest in R2, decreasing by 7.29%, 10.70% and 14.75% 
compared with R1, R3, and R4, respectively. Conversely, Bacteroidota, 
Desulfobacterota I, Actinobacteriota, and Firmicutes A were markedly 
enriched in R2, reaching approximately tenfold the levels observed in 
the other reactors. These phyla have been associated with the conver­
sion of organic compounds into VFAs [4]. The pronounced shift in 
community structure therefore suggested that the R2 hydrodynamic 
condition selectively favored microbial populations potentially involved 
in organic matter conversion rather than simply increasing the overall 
abundance of a single dominant phylum.
At the genus level, R2 was enriched in several facultative, hydrolytic, 
and acidogenic genera (Fig. 5b), including Klebsiella (35.79%), Bacter­
oides (7.77%), Propionivibrio (6.62%), and Enterobacter (5.20%). Klebsi­
ella and Enterobacter were associated with azo reduction and VFA 
production, whereas Bacteroides and Propionivibrio contributed to 
macromolecular organic matter hydrolysis and propionate fermenta­
tion, respectively [44–47]. Bacillus, Brooklawnia, and Macellibacteroides 
were also enriched in R2. The association network linked these func­
tional genera with oxygen transfer and treatment indicators (Fig. 5c), 
supporting their potential roles in dye transformation and acidogenesis.
These community shifts corresponded with the oxygen transfer and 
treatment responses. R1 had the lowest DO and OTR and relatively high 
abundances of Plasticicumulans (9.72%), Pseudomonas (7.88%), Klebsi­
ella (6.52%), and Desulfobulbus (6.10%). In R2, the low DO (0.14 
± 0.02 mg/L) combined with a relatively high OTR (1.37 mg/(L⋅h)) 
coincided with the enrichment of facultative, hydrolytic, and acidogenic 
bacteria and higher VFA production. Although OTR remained at a 
similar level in R3, the increased DO was accompanied by decreased 
abundances of Bacteroides, Enterobacter, Propionivibrio, and Bacillus. 
These genera also remained less abundant in R4, which exhibited the 
highest DO but a lower OTR. Meanwhile, decolorization remained 
consistently high across R1-R4. These results indicated that R2 provided 
favorable micro-aerobic conditions for the coexistence of hydrolytic and

3.7. Metabolic pathways
KEGG functional annotation of the metagenomic data was performed 
to identify key metabolic pathways. Metabolism dominated the anno­
tated functions at level 1, while carbohydrate metabolism was the most 
abundant pathway at level 2 and peaked in R2 (Fig. S6). KEGG level 3 
analysis identified pathways associated with Acid Red degradation and 
acidogenesis (Fig. 6). Nitrogen metabolism (ko00910) was highly 
abundant across all reactors, suggesting a potential link with azo bond 
cleavage and the high decolorization efficiency shown in Fig. 3a. Aro­
matic compound degradation pathways, including benzoate degrada­
tion (ko00362), aminobenzoate degradation (ko00627), and polycyclic 
aromatic hydrocarbon degradation (ko00624), suggested potential 
involvement in the transformation of aromatic intermediates following 
azo reduction. These pathways were further connected with pyruvate 
metabolism (ko00620) and VFA production related metabolism, such as 
propanoate metabolism (ko00640), both of which were relatively 
enriched in R2 and consistent with the increased propionate production 
(Fig. 3f). Meanwhile, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis (ko00010), the TCA 
cycle (ko00020), and amino acid metabolism (ko00350, ko00360 and 
ko00380) may regulate the supply and consumption of carbon in­
termediates during these processes, thereby maintaining metabolic 
balance [48]. The enrichment of sulfur metabolism (ko00920) further 
suggested the potential transformation of sulfonic groups derived from 
Acid Red. These results suggested that Acid Red transformation was 
associated with nitrogen and sulfur metabolism, aromatic compound 
degradation, pyruvate metabolism, acidogenic metabolism, central 
carbon metabolism, and amino acid metabolism. However, the specific 
degradation route and catalytic steps require further resolution through 
key enzyme-encoding genes analysis.

3.8. Microbial metabolic functions and dye degradation pathways
Based on the functional group response sequence (Section 3.5), key 
enzyme-encoding genes, and metabolites identified by LC-MS, a poten­
tial pathway for Acid Red GR degradation and acidogenesis in the 
MAHA system was proposed (Figs. 7a-7b). Acid Red GR transformation 
was proposed to involve azo bond cleavage, aromatic intermediate 
transformation, desulfonation, ring cleavage, pyruvate generation and 
VFA formation.
As shown in Fig. 7a, genes encoding FMN-dependent NADH-azor­
eductase (EC:1.7.1.17) were relatively abundant across all reactors, 
suggesting functional potential for reductive azo-bond cleavage. 
Although oxygen can inhibit azoreductase activity by competing for 
reducing equivalents [49], microscale DO profiles revealed anaerobic 
microzones within the carrier-associated biofilms (Fig. S7), providing 
favorable local conditions for azo reduction despite bulk DO of 
0.11–0.24 mg/L. Genes annotated as nitroreductase/dihydropteridine 
reductase (EC:1.5.1.34) further supported the reductive potential of the 
microbial communities, consistent with the high decolorization effi­
ciencies (Fig. 3a). Genes encoding anthranilate 1,2-dioxygenase 
(EC:1.14.12.1 
and 
EC:1.18.1.-) 
and 
phenol 
hydroxylase 
(EC:1.14.13.244 and EC:1.14.13.-) suggested potential for further 
transformation of aromatic amine and phenolic intermediates toward 
catechol (C00090). Hydroquinone (C00530) was also detected by LC-MS 
(Fig. 7c), although its downstream transformation was less clearly sup­
ported by enzyme annotations.
Based on pathway annotation, catechol could undergo ortho cleav­
age via catechol 1,2-dioxygenase (EC:1.13.11.1) to form cis,cis- 
muconate (C02480), followed by conversion to 3-oxoadipate (C00846) 
and succinyl-CoA (C00091). Alternatively, meta cleavage via catechol 
2,3-dioxygenase (EC:1.13.11.2) could yield 2-hydroxymuconate semi­
aldehyde (C00682) and subsequently enter pyruvate metabolism. Genes 
associated with meta cleavage and pyruvate formation were more 
abundant in R2, suggesting greater potential for channeling aromatic 
intermediates toward acidogenic metabolism. For sulfonated aromatic 
intermediates, LC-MS identified 1-naphthol-5-sulfonic acid and the 
structurally related non-sulfonated intermediate 1-naphthol (C11714), 
together with intermediates associated with subsequent aromatic 
transformation and ring cleavage (Table S3). Notably, no ring-cleavage 
products retaining sulfonate groups were detected. These findings sug­
gested that sulfonated aromatic intermediates underwent desulfonation 
before ring cleavage and subsequently entered catechol metabolism.
Pyruvate is a key precursor for acidogenic fermentation [50] and can 
be converted to acetyl-CoA and subsequently to acetate through several 
enzymatic steps (Fig. 7b). The relatively high abundance of 
acetate-forming enzyme genes was consistent with the dominance of 
acetate among VFAs. In R2, enrichment of genes encoding 
propionate-related enzymes (EC:2.3.1.8 and EC:2.8.3.18) and in­
termediates, including malonyl-CoA and propanoyl-CoA, coincided with 
the highest propionate production (Fig. 3f), suggesting enhanced pro­
pionate fermentation. In contrast, the low abundance of downstream 
butyrate-pathway enzyme genes was consistent with limited butyrate 
formation.
Glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, the TCA cycle, and amino acid meta­
bolism were interconnected through central metabolites such as pyru­
vate and acetyl-CoA, linking aromatic degradation with acidogenic 
metabolism. Genes associated with the TCA cycle and amino acid 
metabolism showed only minor differences among reactors (Fig. 7d), 
whereas several glycolytic and pyruvate-forming enzyme genes were 
relatively enriched in R2. These patterns suggested a greater metabolic 
potential for channeling carbon toward pyruvate in R2, thereby sup­
porting the connection between aromatic intermediate transformation 
and VFA formation.
3.9. Integrated association analysis
To further explore the integrated association, genes annotated as 
encoding key enzymes potentially involved in Acid Red GR trans­
formation and acidogenesis, and their top ten contributing genera were 
identified (Fig. S8). A microbe-enzyme-metabolite correlation network 
was then constructed (Fig. 8a). Cross-group correlations (150) were 
markedly more frequent than within-group correlations (83), and posi­
tive correlations predominated (61.83%). This suggested coordinated 
associations among functional microorganisms, enzyme-encoding 
genes, and metabolite profiles during Acid Red GR transformation and 
VFA formation.
Bacteroides, Klebsiella, Propionivibrio, Bacillus, and Pseudomonas were 
identified as key genera linking enzyme modules with metabolite vari­
ations. Among them, Pseudomonas was strongly correlated with aro­
matic transformation-related enzymes (r > 0.783) and intermediates 
such as hydroquinone (r > 0.817), suggesting potential involvement in 
aromatic intermediate transformation. In contrast, Bacteroides, Propio­
nivibrio, and Bacillus were closely associated with enzymes related to 
acidogenesis and central carbon metabolism (r > 0.794), supporting 
their potential roles in linking aromatic degradation products with VFA 
formation. Notably, Klebsiella-associated enzyme modules showed con­
trasting correlations with 4-aminophenol and hydroquinone, suggesting 
a complex relationship between Klebsiella and aromatic intermediate 
transformation.
Mantel tests were used to assess relationships between environ­
mental factors and microbial metabolic responses (Fig. 8b). Turbulence 
intensity was significantly associated with functional microorganisms 
and key enzyme-encoding genes, which were also positively correlated 
with oxygen transfer parameters (kLa, SOTR, SOTE, and OTR). The re­
sults indicated that the flow regime was associated with shifts in mi­
crobial composition and enzyme-encoding gene profiles related to 
hydrolysis and acidogenesis. However, flow parameters were not 
significantly correlated with oxygen transfer, indicating that oxygen 
transfer characteristics were not determined by turbulence intensity 
alone. R1 exhibited a relatively uniform but weak flow field, whereas R3 
and R4 showed stronger but more heterogeneous turbulence. R2 com­
bined relatively uniform flow with moderate intensity, consistent with 
its favorable oxygen-transfer and acidogenic responses. Metabolites 
showed comparatively weak correlations with oxygen-transfer param­
eters and VFAs, suggesting that their profiles reflected multiple pro­
cesses of formation, transformation, and consumption rather than 
oxygen transfer alone.
3.10. Potential mechanisms of hydrodynamic regulation in the MAHA 
system
Based on these results, a potential mechanism linking flow regime, 
oxygen mass transfer, dye degradation, hydrolysis acidification, and 
microbial metabolism in the MAHA systems was proposed (Fig. 8c). R2 
combined appropriate turbulence intensity with greater flow uniformity 
and maintained relatively high oxygen transfer performance (kLa and 
OTR). This hydrodynamic condition was associated with the coexistence 
of facultative anaerobic and fermentative bacteria, including Bacter­
oides, Klebsiella, Propionivibrio, Bacillus, Enterobacter, and Brooklawnia. 
The enrichment of these functional taxa was accompanied by higher 
abundances of genes encoding enzymes related to azo-bond reduction, 
aromatic intermediate transformation, and acidogenic metabolism, 
thereby promoting Acid Red GR decolorization, aromatic intermediate 
conversion, biodegradability improvement, and VFA production.
Although the synthetic wastewater was designed to reflect real 
dyeing wastewater, it cannot fully capture its compositional complexity 
and temporal variability. Nevertheless, the controlled matrix enabled 
reliable elucidation of the relationships among hydrodynamics, oxygen 
transfer, microbial metabolism, and Acid Red GR transformation. Future 
studies should validate these mechanisms using real wastewater under

4. Conclusion
This study demonstrated that hydrodynamic regulation was an 
important factor controlling oxygen transfer, microbial adaptation, and 
Acid Red GR transformation in the MAHA reactor. Moderate stirring 
intensity (R2, 120 rad/min) established a favorable low-oxygen micro­
environment by balancing turbulence enhancement and flow unifor­
mity, thereby improving biodegradability and acidogenic conversion 
while maintaining efficient decolorization. Multi-scale analyses indi­
cated that this condition promoted the formation of a stable EPS matrix, 
enriched facultative hydrolytic and acidogenic microorganisms, and 
enhanced functional potentials associated with azo-dye transformation 
and carbon metabolism. Integrating LC-MS, FTIR/2D-COS, and micro­
bial functional information, a potential Acid Red GR transformation 
pathway involving azo-bond reduction, aromatic structure trans­
formation, and subsequent acidogenesis was proposed. These findings 
highlight that optimizing hydrodynamic conditions, rather than simply 
increasing oxygen supply, is a promising strategy for regulating micro­
bial metabolism and enhancing MAHA performance in dyeing waste­
water treatment.
Environmental implication
Acid Red GR is a hazardous azo dye because its chromophoric azo 
bonds, sulfonated aromatic structures, and aromatic amine-derived in­
termediates make dyeing wastewater persistent, colored, and poten­
tially toxic. This work shows that hydrodynamic regulation in a 
microaerobic hydrolysis acidification reactor can steer oxygen transfer, 
enrich facultative fermentative bacteria, and activate enzymes for azo 
reduction, desulfonation, aromatic ring cleavage, and acidogenesis. By 
converting refractory dye-derived organics into more biodegradable 
products and VFAs under moderate stirring, the study provides an 
operational strategy for improving industrial dyeing wastewater pre­
treatment and reducing environmental risks from hazardous organic 
pollutants.
